In brief

Indulging several warm appreciations of Cissy Caffrey, the narrator of Nausicaa recalls an incident of cross-dressing: "O, and will you ever forget the evening she dressed up in her father's suit and hat and the burned cork moustache and walked down Tritonville road, smoking a cigarette. There was none to come up to her for fun." This incident was inspired by Joyce's lover Nora Barnacle, who as a girl in Galway had boldly gone out at night in men's clothes. Within the fictive confines of the novel, it seems to anticipate later passages which suggest that Cissy ignores conventional sexual morality in even more daring, and less cute, ways.

At more length

Nora was a highspirited young woman, and she chafed at the restraints her family attempted to impose on her. Brenda Maddox tells how she dodged a violently repressive maternal uncle:

    It fell to Tom Healy, prompted perhaps by his new wife, Bedelia, to try to discipline his adventurous niece. He took to walking around Galway at night, swinging his blackthorn stick and looking for Nora. As he prowled, he whistled the Irish air 'My Mountain Maid, Arise'. Nora froze in dread when she heard it floating through the night.
    Nora would not be kept in. With her best friend, Mary O'Holleran, she found ways to escape. With Mary, she would dress up in men's clothes, hair tucked under a man's cap, and explore the streets of Galway and Eyre Square. Nora had the height, the swagger, the confidence, and the heavy brows to pass in the dark for a good-sized boy. Once they even spotted the dreaded Uncle Tommy; Mary said 'Good evening' in a deep false voice and got away with it. (Nora 18)

Joyce's fictionalized version sets the adventure on "Tritonville Road," the main drag running north from Sandymount to Irishtown. He omits the threatening uncle but adds a "burned cork moustache" straight out of the minstrel shows (Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner document the use of this substance in blackface acts), and also a cigarette. The annotators observe that female smoking was frowned on throughout the 19th century and only slowly began to gain acceptance in the early 20th century. Outside of music halls the taboo against cross-dressing was also strong, as Maddox notes. But the photographs reproduced here suggest that many women were drawn to it.

Nausicaa thus hints that Cissy Caffrey defies conventional sexual morality much more directly than her friend Gerty does: Gerty upholds the stereotypes of female beauty while allowing one man to think of her as not fully chaste, but Cissy steps quite literally out of the stereotypes and walks her own way. Apparently she does so not only by wearing men's clothes, but also in other kinds of evening jaunts. The opening pages of the Circe episode show her walking the streets of the red-light district in the company of two British soldiers, singing verses of a lewd ditty: "I gave it to Molly / Because she was jolly, / The leg of the duck [...] I gave it to Nelly / To stick in her belly, / The leg of the duck [...] She has it, she got it, / Wherever she put it, / The leg of the duck." Much later in the chapter she is still with the soldiers when they try to pick a fight with Stephen, accusing him of insulting their girl. She is alarmed but also thrilled: "They're going to fight. For me!"

After the comfortably domestic scene in Nausicaa—unmarried girls keeping their own company, nice clothes, babysitting, anodyne prose—this is so shocking as to seem unbelievable. And perhaps it is unbelievable: in Circe the boundaries between actual events and hallucinatory ones are never quite clear. But it becomes hard to interpret Cissy as merely the figment of someone's imagination when Bloom shakes her by the shoulders imploring her to talk sense to the soldiers ("Speak, you! Are you struck dumb? You are the link between nations and generations. Speak, woman, sacred lifegiver!"), when Cissy clings to one of the soldiers' sleeves ("Amn't I with you? Amn't I your girl? Cissy's your girl"), when Stephen savors her sex appeal ("White thy fambles, red thy gan / And thy quarrons dainty is"), and when Cissy finally does as Bloom has asked ("Come on, you're boosed. He insulted me but I forgive him"). Collectively, all these actions suggest that Cissy is "really" there just as much as Stephen, Bloom, and the soldiers are—no matter how fantastic some of their words may sound.

Cissy says "I'm only a shilling whore." If this statement is a product of the chapter's phantasmagoric inventions, then perhaps she is only "Slumming" in Nighttown, as Bloom says Molly has often wanted to do. But walking with two soldiers at night—anywhere, much less this part of town—clearly shows that she is not constrained by middle-class sexual expectations. Elsewhere in Nausicaa Gerty scorns such women as "fallen": "She loathed that sort of person, the fallen women off the accommodation walk beside the Dodder that went with the soldiers and coarse men with no respect for a girl's honour, degrading the sex and being taken up to the police station." Cissy steps much farther away from home than the Tritonville Road—down to the Dodder and on north to the Monto—and much further away from bourgeois propriety than simply trying on her father's suit.

John Hunt 2026

title: Her father's suit
